content: The systematic review process began with the formulation of a clear PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) question. This included defining criteria for identifying studies, developing search strategies for various bibliographic databases, establishing methods for assessing the risk of bias, and creating a detailed data analysis plan. The protocol was reviewed and approved by the Steering Group and selected content experts from the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The development of the systematic review was iterative, with methodologists maintaining constant communication with the Steering Group to address challenges and agree on solutions. Qualitative reviews focused on several key areas: understanding what aspects of intrapartum care matter most to women and healthcare providers, identifying barriers and facilitators to the adoption and delivery of intrapartum care interventions, assessing the acceptability of practices to women and healthcare professionals, evaluating the feasibility of implementing interventions, and determining how outcomes influenced by an intervention are valued by women and other stakeholders. Additionally, perceptions of equity related to prioritized interventions were explored. Qualitative evidence on labor companionship and respectful maternity care (RMC) was derived from two specific qualitative systematic reviews. To address the question of effective communication by healthcare providers, a mixed-methods review was conducted. The search strategies for identifying and retrieving evidence for these reviews are detailed in the respective publications. Evidence on cost-effectiveness was obtained through a systematic review of the literature from January 1, 1996, to February 20, 2017, using the MEDLINE electronic database. This review retrieved data on the costs and cost-effectiveness of intrapartum care in general, as well as specific interventions such as fetal monitoring, clinical pelvimetry, communication, companionship, birth positions, episiotomy, and pain relief methods. The related articles feature in PubMed was also used to identify additional relevant studies. The quality of primary studies included in the reviews was assessed using explicit methods for risk-of-bias evaluation, as outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Each study was rated as having low, high, or unclear risk of bias based on six standard criteria: sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of study personnel and participants, attrition, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias, such as publication bias. This assessment provided an overall risk of bias for each study, indicating the likely magnitude and direction of the bias and its potential impact on the review findings. For new systematic reviews on the effectiveness of interventions commissioned by the WHO Steering Group, the Cochrane methodology was used to assess the risk of bias. Studies included in qualitative reviews underwent a simpler quality appraisal system using a validated instrument that rated studies against 11 predefined criteria. These studies were then assigned a score ranging from A to D, with D indicating significant flaws likely to affect the credibility, transferability, dependability, and/or confirmability of the study. Studies scoring D were excluded due to poor quality. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) approach was used to appraise the quality of quantitative evidence for all critical outcomes identified in the PICO questions. A GRADE evidence profile was prepared for each quantitative outcome for each priority question. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on specific criteria. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were considered to provide high-certainty evidence by default, while non-randomized trials and observational studies provided low-certainty evidence. The baseline quality rating could be downgraded based on study design limitations (risk of bias), inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. For observational studies, other considerations, such as the magnitude of effect, could lead to an upgraded rating if no limitations necessitated downgrading. The systematic review teams and methodologists from the Cochrane Review Editorial Process (CREP) graded the quantitative review evidence following standard operating procedures approved by the WHO Steering Group. The findings of the qualitative reviews were appraised for quality using the GRADE-CERQual (Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research) tool. This tool provides a transparent method for assessing and assigning the level of confidence in evidence from qualitative research reviews. The systematic review team used the GRADE-CERQual tool to assess confidence in qualitative review findings, assigning a level of confidence to evidence domains such as values, acceptability, and feasibility based on four components: methodological limitations of individual studies, adequacy of data, coherence, and relevance to the review question. The WHO Steering Group supervised and finalized the preparation of evidence profiles and summaries in collaboration with the Technical Working Group (TWG) using the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework. The EtD tool systematically considered evidence on prioritized interventions across specified domains, including effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. For each priority question, judgments were made on the impact of the intervention on each domain to guide the decision-making process. Using the EtD framework template, the Steering Group and TWG created summary documents for each priority question, covering evidence on each domain. When benefits clearly outweighed harms for outcomes highly valued by pregnant women, or vice versa, a clear judgment in favor of or against the intervention was more likely. Uncertainty about net benefits or harms, or small net benefits, typically led to a judgment that did not favor the intervention or comparator. Higher certainty of evidence of benefits across outcomes increased the likelihood of a judgment in favor of the intervention. In the absence of evidence of benefits, evidence of potential harm led to a recommendation against the option. The values domain considered the relative importance assigned to the outcomes of the intervention by those affected, how this importance varied across settings, and whether there was uncertainty surrounding this importance. Interventions resulting in outcomes consistently valued by most women, regardless of settings, were more likely to lead to a judgment in favor of the intervention. This domain, along with the effects domain, informed the balance of effects judgment. The resources required to implement the reviewed intrapartum care interventions included costs for supplies, training, equipment, and skilled human resources. A judgment in favor of or against the intervention was likely when resource implications were clearly advantageous or disadvantageous, respectively. Cost evaluation relied on reported estimates obtained during the evidence retrieval process, the One Health Model, the WHO compendium of innovative health technologies for low-resource settings, and the experiences and opinions of GDG members. Where available, direct evidence from systematic reviews of cost-effectiveness informed this domain. Qualitative evidence from systematic reviews on women's and providers' views and experiences across different labor practices informed judgments for the acceptability and feasibility domains. Lower acceptability reduced the likelihood of a judgment in favor of the intervention. If an intervention associated with low acceptability was recommended, the recommendation was accompanied by a strategy to address acceptability concerns during implementation. The feasibility of implementing an intervention depended on factors such as resources, infrastructure, and training requirements. Where barriers were identified, a judgment in favor of the intervention was less likely. The equity domain encompassed evidence or considerations regarding whether an intervention would reduce health inequities. Findings from qualitative systematic reviews, the 2015 WHO report on inequalities in reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health, a review on facilitators and barriers to facility-based birth, and the experiences and opinions of GDG members informed this domain. An intervention was likely to be recommended if its proven or anticipated effects reduced health inequalities among different groups of women and their families. For each domain, additional evidence of potential harms or unintended consequences was described in the additional considerations subsections. These considerations were derived from studies that might not have directly addressed the priority question but provided relevant information in the absence of direct evidence. These were extracted from single studies, systematic reviews, or other relevant sources. The WHO Steering Group provided the EtD frameworks, including evidence summaries, GRADE evidence profiles, and other documents related to each recommendation, to GDG members as soon as the documents were drafted and several weeks in advance of face-to-face meetings. GDG members were asked to review and electronically provide comments on the documents before the meetings. During the face-to-face meetings at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, in May and September 2017, under the leadership of the GDG chairperson, members collectively reviewed the frameworks, draft recommendations, and any comments received through preliminary feedback. The purpose of the meetings was to reach consensus on each recommendation, including its direction and, in some instances, the specific context, based on explicit consideration of the range of evidence presented in each EtD framework and the judgment of GDG members. In line with other recently published WHO guidelines using EtD frameworks, the GDG classified each recommendation into one of the following categories: Recommended, Not recommended, Recommended only in specific contexts, or Recommended only in the context of rigorous research. For integrated recommendations from existing guidelines, information on the strength and quality of the evidence from the source guideline document was presented in the accompanying remarks. For consistency, integrated recommendations were also categorized according to the typology described above. The GDG meetings followed a protocol designed to allow participants to discuss the supporting evidence and each of the recommendations drafted by the WHO Steering Group and to reach a consensus on the final wording of each recommendation after revision. Consensus was defined as agreement by three-quarters or more of the GDG, provided that those who disagreed did not feel strongly about their position. Strong disagreements would have been recorded in the guideline, but no such disagreements were noted in any of the GDG meetings. Where required, the GDG determined the context of recommendations by the same process of consensus, based on discussions about the balance of evidence on the effects (benefits and harms) of the interventions across different contexts. If participants were unable to reach a consensus, the disputed recommendation or decision would be put to a vote. Voting would have been conducted by a show of hands among GDG members. A recommendation or decision would stand if more than two-thirds of the GDG voted in support of it, unless the disagreement was related to a safety concern, in which case the WHO Secretariat could choose not to issue a recommendation on the subject. WHO staff at the meetings, external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading, and observers were not eligible to vote. If the issue to be voted upon involved primary research or systematic reviews conducted by any participants who had declared an academic conflict of interest, those individuals were allowed to participate in the discussion but were not allowed to vote on the issue in question. In accordance with the WHO handbook for guideline development, all GDG, TWG, and ERG members, as well as external collaborators, were required to declare in writing any competing interests (academic, financial, or other) at the time of their invitation to participate in the guideline development process. The standard WHO form for declaration of interests (DOI) was completed and signed by each expert and submitted electronically to the responsible technical officer. The WHO Steering Group reviewed all DOI forms before finalizing experts' invitations to participate.
